say.text: Welcome to Class 59. Today we look at the big ideas and inventions that changed the 1900s. We will take them one at a time, and slowly.

show.text: 20th-Century Science and Technology

say.text: Six topics: quantum theory and relativity, antibiotics and vaccines, the shape of DNA, computers and networks, the Green Revolution, and how we learned the Big Bang story.

show.text:
1. Quantum theory and relativity
2. Antibiotics and vaccines
3. The shape of DNA
4. Computers and early networks
5. The Green Revolution
6. Back to the Big Bang

say.text: First, quantum theory. Picture a staircase, not a smooth ramp. In 1900 Max Planck proposed that energy is given off in small units called quanta.

show.text: Quantum: a tiny packet of energy

say.text: Five years later Einstein used Planck's idea to explain the photoelectric effect, an odd experimental result. He went further than Planck and treated light itself as coming in packets.

show.text: A staircase drawn next to a smooth ramp. Energy moves in steps, like the staircase.

ask.q: Which picture matches the quantum idea?
ask.right: A staircase: energy comes in small steps.
wrong: A smooth ramp: energy changes by any tiny amount.
A circle: energy goes round and round.
A mirror: energy bounces back.
ask.why: Planck proposed that energy is given off in small units called quanta, so it changes in steps, like a staircase.

say.text: Quantum theory soon reached the atom itself. By then it was no longer a side issue in physics. It was becoming the main story.

show.text: Quantum theory and the atom

say.text: Now relativity, from the same Einstein. He published special relativity in 1905 and general relativity in 1915.

show.text:
1905: special relativity
1915: general relativity
1919: the eclipse test

say.text: Special relativity could not handle gravity. General relativity could. Its big idea: the Sun's mass curves space around it, so starlight passing close by bends.

show.text: A heavy ball on a stretched sheet makes a dip. A marble rolls around the dip.

say.text: A good theory must predict something new. In May 1919, British expeditions watched a total solar eclipse. They checked whether stars near the Sun seemed to move.

show.text: The 1919 eclipse path crossed the equator from South America to Uganda.

say.text: The stars had shifted just as Einstein predicted. He became world-famous almost at once.

show.text: 1919: starlight bends near the Sun

ask.right: Whether the Sun's gravity bends starlight.
wrong: How old the Sun is.
Whether energy comes in steps called quanta.
How far away the stars are.
ask.why: General relativity predicted that light bends in a gravitational field. The eclipse let astronomers photograph stars near the Sun and check.

say.text: Next, medicine. An antibiotic is a medicine that fights bacteria. The first widely used one was penicillin, which comes from a mould.

show.text: Antibiotic: a medicine against bacteria

say.text: In September 1928 Alexander Fleming came back from holiday. He found that bacteria had failed to grow around a mould that had landed on one of his dishes.

show.text: A round dish of bacteria with a clear ring around a patch of green mould.

say.text: Fleming did not see how important it was. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain showed in 1940 that it could treat many diseases. By 1941 an injectable form was available.

show.text:
1928: Fleming sees the mould
1940: Florey and Chain show it works
1941: injectable form
1945: Nobel Prize for all three

ask.q: Who showed that penicillin could work as a medicine?
wrong: Fleming alone, on the day he saw the mould.
Nobody. It was never used as a medicine.
The astronomers of the 1919 eclipse.
ask.why: Fleming noticed the mould in 1928, but Florey and Chain showed in 1940 that penicillin could treat many bacterial diseases.

say.text: One caution. Some bacteria have since become resistant to penicillin. A medicine that works is not a medicine that works forever.

show.text: Resistance: some bacteria survive the drug

say.text: Now vaccines. Before them, the only protection against many diseases was surviving the infection. A vaccine trains the body ahead of time, safely.

show.text: Vaccine: practice for the body's defences

say.text: Polio was feared. Jonas Salk made a vaccine from killed virus, which cannot cause the disease. In April 1955 a trial reported it safe and about 90 percent effective against paralysis.

show.text: April 12, 1955: Salk vaccine reported safe and 90% effective

say.text: Albert Sabin took another path: a live but weakened virus. It was easier to give, especially in poorer countries, and it followed in the early 1960s.

show.text: Salk: killed virus, injected | Sabin: live weakened virus, easier to give

ask.q: Which vaccine used a live, weakened virus?
wrong: Salk's vaccine.
Fleming's penicillin.
Neither used a virus.
ask.why: Salk used killed virus. Sabin used a live but weakened virus, which is why it was easier to give.

say.text: Vaccines' greatest win was smallpox. The World Health Organization began an intensified campaign in 1967, and in 1980 smallpox was declared eradicated.

show.text:
1967: intensified campaign begins
1980: smallpox declared eradicated
1988: polio campaign begins

say.text: Eradication means more than clearing one town. The WHO defines it as a permanent reduction to zero, with no risk of the disease coming back.

show.text: Eradication: permanently zero

ask.q: What does eradication of a disease mean?
ask.right: Permanent reduction to zero by deliberate effort, with no risk of its return.
wrong: The disease is gone from one town for a year.
Everyone has been vaccinated once.
Cases have fallen by half.
ask.why: The WHO defines eradication as permanent reduction to zero, with no more risk of reintroduction. That is more than clearing it from one area.

say.text: Smallpox was a good target for three reasons. It only infected humans, its symptoms were easy to spot, and its vaccine was cheap and effective.

show.text:
Only infected humans
Easy to recognise
Cheap, effective vaccine

say.text: Now DNA. It is the molecule that helps pass life's instructions from parents to children. Its shape was the great puzzle of the early 1950s.

show.text: DNA: the molecule of inheritance

say.text: The answer was a double helix: two strands wound round each other, like a twisted ladder.

show.text: A twisted ladder: two long spiral strands joined by rungs.

say.text: The clue was an X-ray picture. In May 1952 Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling took Photograph 51 at King's College London. Its pattern of spots strongly suggests a helix.

show.text: A grey X-ray image with a dark X shape of spots, known as Photograph 51.

say.text: In April 1953 Watson and Crick published their model in the journal Nature. Franklin and Gosling's paper, with the photograph, appeared in the same issue.

show.text:
May 1952: Photograph 51
April 1953: Watson and Crick's model; Franklin and Gosling's paper
1962: Nobel Prize to Watson, Crick and Wilkins

ask.q: What did Photograph 51 suggest about DNA?
ask.right: That DNA has a helical shape.
wrong: That DNA is a flat sheet.
That DNA is a single straight line.
That DNA is a closed ring.
ask.why: The pattern of spots in the X-ray image strongly suggests a helix, which led to the double-helix model.

say.text: Franklin died in 1958, and the 1962 Nobel Prize went to Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins. How credit was shared is still discussed, and we come back to it at the end.

show.text: Credit: see 'The other side'

say.text: A frame of reference. In 1953 Stalin died in March, Everest was first climbed on 29 May, Elizabeth II was crowned on 2 June, and the Korean War armistice came in July.

show.text:
March 1953: Stalin dies
29 May: Everest first climbed
2 June: Elizabeth II crowned
27 July: Korean armistice

say.text: Now computers. A computer follows a list of instructions, a program, to calculate automatically. A famous early one was ENIAC at the University of Pennsylvania.

show.text: ENIAC: early electronic computer

say.text: The US Army needed ENIAC to work out artillery firing tables. It was finished too late for the war. Its first big job, in December 1945, was a problem for the hydrogen bomb.

show.text: Built 1943 to 1946 for the US Army

say.text: It was huge. The machine had 40 panels, each nine feet tall. Technicians set it up for a job by rewiring its connections.

show.text: 40 panels, each nine feet tall

ask.q: What was ENIAC built to do?
ask.right: Calculate artillery firing tables for the US Army.
wrong: Send messages between universities.
Cure bacterial infections.
Measure the bending of starlight.
ask.why: The military needed ENIAC to calculate ballistic tables, which are the firing tables used by artillery crews.

say.text: A frame of reference. In 1945 penicillin's three pioneers won their Nobel Prize and ENIAC did its first big job. In 1955 the Salk vaccine arrived, and ENIAC's long run ended that October.

show.text:
1945: Nobel for penicillin; ENIAC's first big job
1955: Salk vaccine; ENIAC retired

say.text: Computers became more useful when joined together. ARPANET was a network funded by the US Defense Department. Its key idea was packet switching.

show.text: Packet switching

say.text: Packet switching breaks information into small bundles. They travel separately and are put back together at the other end.

show.text: A long letter cut into small cards, sent in separate envelopes, then reassembled.

ask.right: Breaking information into small bundles that are sent and put back together.
wrong: Sending a whole message down one unbroken wire.
Writing messages on paper and posting them.
Switching a computer off and on.
ask.why: Packet switching breaks information into smaller bundles that are easier to transmit and are reassembled at the receiving end.

say.text: On 29 October 1969, at 10:30 at night, a UCLA student tried to log in to a computer at Stanford Research Institute. Only the first two letters got through before it crashed.

show.text: First message: lo

say.text: That was three months after people first walked on the Moon. ARPANET began with four computers. It grew over two decades and was folded into the wider internet.

show.text:
July 1969: Moon landing
Oct 1969: first ARPANET message
1989: ARPANET shut down

say.text: The internet gets its own story in Class 61. For now, on to food and the Green Revolution.

show.text: The Green Revolution

say.text: Norman Borlaug worked in Mexico from 1944. A fungus disease called rust was ruining wheat crops. He crossbred wheat to make types that resisted rust and gave more grain.

show.text: A wheat field with tall, thin stalks beside shorter, sturdier ones.

say.text: He crossed his wheat with a Japanese dwarf wheat. The result was shorter, so it would not tip over under heavy grain, and it responded well to fertiliser.

show.text: Semi-dwarf wheat

ask.right: It was less likely to tip over under heavy grain.
wrong: It needed no water at all.
It could grow in the dark.
It was bred to feed insects.
ask.why: Shorter plants did not tip over under the extra grain at the top, and the new wheat was disease-resistant and responded well to fertiliser.

say.text: In 1966 India imported 18,000 tons of the Mexican dwarf wheat seed. India's wheat harvest rose from 12.3 million tons in 1965 to 20 million in 1970.

show.text: Wheat harvests, 1965 and 1970

say.text: Pakistan's wheat also nearly doubled in those years. Borlaug won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. One estimate says his work saved about a billion people from starvation.

show.text: Estimated: 1 billion lives

say.text: A frame of reference: Borlaug was born in 1914, the same year as Jonas Salk. Two people from that one year changed how the world fights hunger and disease.

show.text: Born in 1914: Salk and Borlaug

say.text: Last, we return to Class 2. How do we know the universe had a beginning? Einstein's relativity gave scientists the tools.

show.text: Back to the Big Bang

say.text: In 1927 Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian scientist and priest, showed that an expanding universe fits Einstein's equations. In 1931 he suggested it began from a single 'primeval atom'.

show.text:
1922: Friedmann's expanding solutions
1927: Lemaitre
1931: 'primeval atom'

say.text: In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther away, the faster. Run that backwards and everything was once closer together.

show.text: Dots on a balloon move apart as it is blown up. Farther dots move apart faster.

ask.right: Galaxies are moving away, and farther ones move faster.
wrong: All galaxies are moving toward us.
All galaxies move at the same speed.
Galaxies never move.
ask.why: Hubble showed that galaxies seemed to recede at speeds proportional to their distance. That fits an expanding universe.

say.text: A rival idea, the Steady State, said matter was created continuously so the universe stayed the same. The two ideas made different predictions.

show.text: Big Bang: hot, dense start | Steady State: unchanging, new matter always appearing

say.text: The Big Bang predicted a faint glow left over from the hot early universe. In 1964, Penzias and Wilson at Bell Labs found unexplained radio noise from every direction.

show.text: Cosmic microwave background

say.text: A Princeton team had been searching for just that glow. Both groups published in 1965. The Steady State idea could not explain it, and the Big Bang became the leading model.

show.text: 1965: the glow is explained

ask.q: What is the cosmic microwave background?
ask.right: A faint glow from every direction, left over from the hot early universe.
wrong: Light from one very bright star.
Radio signals from a nearby planet.
The sound of the Sun.
ask.why: The Big Bang predicted leftover heat from a hot, dense beginning, and Penzias and Wilson found it as faint radiation coming from all directions.

say.text: Lemaitre died in 1966, three days after hearing of the discovery. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended calling the law of expansion the Hubble-Lemaitre law.

show.text: Hubble-Lemaitre law

say.text: Three pillars now support the Big Bang story: the universe's expansion, the amounts of light elements, and the microwave glow. That is the evidence behind Class 2.

show.text:
1. The universe is expanding
2. The amounts of light elements
3. The cosmic microwave background

say.text: Let us put the century on one line. Each date is one idea from today.

show.text:
1900 Planck's quanta
1905/1915 relativity
1928 penicillin noticed
1929 galaxies receding
1945 ENIAC
1953 DNA double helix
1955 Salk vaccine
1965 cosmic glow
1969 first ARPANET message
1980 smallpox eradicated

ask.right: The DNA double helix was announced.
wrong: The first ARPANET message was sent.
Smallpox was declared eradicated.
Penicillin was first noticed.
ask.why: Watson and Crick published the double helix in April 1953. The ARPANET message was in 1969, smallpox eradication in 1980, and penicillin was noticed in 1928.

say.text: Next time, Class 60: the end of the Cold War, and how the world changed afterwards. Well done for staying with six big ideas.

show.text: Next: Class 60, The End of the Cold War

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Stalin died on 5 March. Hillary and Tenzing reached the top of Everest on 29 May, and the news reached London on the morning of the coronation. Elizabeth II was crowned on 2 June, in the first coronation broadcast live on television. The Korean War armistice was signed on 27 July.

frame_of_reference.when: 1945 (penicillin Nobel Prize; ENIAC's first big job)
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The Second World War was ending. ENIAC was finished too late for the war, and its first big job was a hydrogen-bomb problem.
Salk's polio vaccine was reported safe on 12 April. Alexander Fleming died that year. ENIAC's long run ended in October.
The message came three months after a human first set foot on the Moon.

frame_of_reference.when: 1914 (births of Jonas Salk and Norman Borlaug)
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Salk (1914 to 1995), who made the first polio vaccine, and Borlaug (born 25 March 1914), who bred the Green Revolution wheat, were born in the same year.

other_side.claim: Max Planck started the quantum revolution in 1900.
other_side.other_view: Historians debate whether Planck saw his 1900 step as the beginning of the end of classical physics. Some argue he treated it as a temporary calculating trick. Einstein's 1905 work treated light itself as quantised, which Planck did not.

other_side.claim: Watson and Crick discovered the structure of DNA.
other_side.other_view: Watson and Crick built the model and shared the 1962 Nobel Prize with Wilkins. But Franklin's Photograph 51 pushed their work forward, and she was unaware it had been shown to Watson. Some recent biographers argue the scientists at the time may have seen the work as collaborative, not as one team's achievement.

other_side.claim: Salk's vaccine was the right way to beat polio.
other_side.other_view: Sabin believed only a live, weakened virus would work. Salk believed a killed virus was safer. Sabin's vaccine was easier to give in poorer countries but can, rarely, cause vaccine-induced polio.

other_side.claim: ENIAC was the first electronic digital computer.
other_side.other_view: ENIAC is widely called the first general-purpose electronic digital computer. A legal ruling, though, gave John Atanasoff recognition as the inventor of the first electronic digital computer.

other_side.claim: The Green Revolution was an unqualified success.
other_side.other_view: Yields in India and Pakistan rose sharply. Some analysts, including a University of Michigan case study, point to costs: reduced crop diversity, more vulnerability to pests and disease, and the loss of local knowledge. Higher yields also depended on fertiliser.

other_side.claim: Hubble discovered that the universe is expanding.
other_side.other_view: Lemaitre reached the same conclusion in 1927, two years before Hubble's 1929 paper. Hubble read the redshifts as real motion, while Lemaitre saw expanding space itself. In 2018 the IAU recommended the name Hubble-Lemaitre law.

other_side.claim: The speed of the universe's expansion is settled.
other_side.other_view: The Big Bang itself is now the leading model, but a detailed number is still argued over. One source notes that finding the Hubble constant is the remaining problem, and that values from the microwave background, around 67, differ from other values.
